The upgraded run will feature an 8-fold increase in luminosity, which is the primary factor limiting performance.  The primary limitation is the readout system's capacity to handle the increase in hit data.  The CMS pixel system's readout has been upgraded with front-end chips that have three readout phases, with the pilot blade being used for beam crossing information and calibration.  The pilot blade data is critical for pixel hit reconstruction and is being reconstructed with a custom algorithm that is being used in the upgraded run.  The reconstruction process is optimized for speed and is being used to process data from collisions at 13 TeV with high luminosity.  The results show that the algorithm can recover a significant amount of beam crossing information and a significant amount of hits, which is a significant improvement over a simple threshold-based reconstruction.  The algorithm is also being further optimized to process data from collisions with high luminosity.

Using a SU(2) gluonium model based on lattice QCD, we have calculated key parameters for a scalar gluonium, including its mass and decay constant, from correlation functions at zero momentum. A K\"all\'en-Lehmann spectral representation is constructed for the scalar gluonium, and the spectral function is derived from QCD at various momentum levels. Our analysis shows that the significant pole in the spectral function corresponds to the gluonium mass, and the residual part of the representation is significant, indicating non-negligent multi-particle contributions. The derived residual part satisfies unitarity constraints, and the significant portion of the spectral function can be attributed to two-gluon states. The obtained one-particle component accounts for approximately half of the completeness relation value at the lowest momentum levels.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on Twitter has become a
popular research topic.  This study introduces a novel sentiment analysis
methodology that leverages Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks.  The
proposed approach is tested on three well-known Twitter sentiment analysis
datasets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness.  The methodology is
further optimized by incorporating part-of-speech (POS) tagging and the use of
GloVe word embeddings.  This study provides a comprehensive comparison of
various sentiment analysis techniques, and the code is made available on GitHub
for open-source collaboration.

A linear charge-accumulation method was employed to derive a non-Abelian charged metric in the Landau-Lifshitz gauge via the Maxwell-Ahn-Chamblin-Henningson (MACH) framework, which corresponds to a theoretically accurate representation of a charged black hole.  Subsequently, a shade transformation was applied to the MACH metric to obtain a non-linear Reissner-Nordstr\"om (RN) metric with a charge-squared form, representing an alternative representation of the same charged black hole.  Although both metrics share the same physical properties, they exhibit different geometries.  Consequently, their respective RNi and MACHi thermodynamic volumes result in different values, which in turn lead to varying Smarr relations.  Notably, the Smarr relation derived from the RNi thermodynamic volume does not conform to the expected form, whereas the MACHi-derived thermodynamic volume does.  To address this discrepancy, the Smarr relation can be recovered by incorporating the work conjugate of the non-linear charge within the RNi framework.

This study investigates the operation of a universal quantum NOT gate using two distinct quantum systems, i.e., qubits, and examines the evolution of entanglement and synchronization through the analysis of their nonlocal tomograms. We leverage the coherence properties of the Heisenberg antiferromagnetic interaction to facilitate the NOT gate's functionality, and observe entanglement creation, partial destruction, and a transition from anti-correlated to correlated states. Our findings demonstrate that tomograms effectively capture these entanglement dynamics and synchronization onsets, providing a viable tool for diagnosing quantum correlations in evolving systems.

Building a dialogue system that adheres to a specific role while engaging with a wide range of topics poses a significant challenge in the field of open-domain conversation research. This study aims to develop a comprehensive approach to constructing a role-specific dialogue system that can maintain consistency in its topic and style across an open-domain conversation. We utilized a large collection of public data to create a new collection, named FARD, that includes over 50,000 conversation turns spanning more than 300 unique personas. We then utilized the Farfield framework, which leverages three key components: a role specification, the FarDataset, and the FarModel, to develop a large-scale role-specific language model. We conducted extensive experiments to assess the FarModel's performance in open-domain dialogue, showing improvements in its ability to maintain a specific role, user satisfaction, and conversation quality. We also carried out additional studies to explore the model's coherence and diversity, as well as its ability to generalize across different conversations.

The choice of pest management tactics is crucial for maintaining high crop yields and quality, ultimately impacting the profitability of agricultural production. Evaluating the effectiveness of these strategies is essential, but the variability of crop yield and revenue due to environmental factors and pests makes this assessment challenging. Our research aims to overcome this challenge by utilizing simulation data to compare the performance of different pest management strategies. We develop a statistical method that accounts for data uncertainty, allowing for a more reliable assessment of strategy effectiveness. This method is demonstrated using strawberry disease management as a case study, where we analyze the performance of various pest management strategies and their impact on crop yield and quality.

Creating 360-degree virtual tours through video requires accurate perspective prediction, which is essential for a realistic and engaging experience.  However, this task becomes more complex when dealing with scenes that contain multiple objects, varying camera settings, and scenes that are not consistent in their layout.  To tackle this challenge, a new dataset is proposed that is specifically designed for predicting perspective in 360-degree virtual tourism videos.  This dataset is unique in its focus and provides a comprehensive set of data for training models.  A new architecture is introduced that is capable of capturing both the foreground and background elements in 360-degree videos.  This model is then enhanced with a subtitle-based attention mechanism that is used to select the relevant areas in the scene.  A new dataset is proposed that is specifically designed for predicting perspective in 360-degree virtual tourism videos.  This data set is unique in its focus and provides a comprehensive set of data for training models.  Experiments on this new dataset and existing benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Tensor network techniques have been extensively utilized to model complex quantum systems, particularly in representing thermal states and system dynamics. However, these methods often encounter difficulties in accurately describing regions of a lattice that are decoupled from one another and their surroundings. A novel tensor method has been developed to tackle thermal states and time evolution in both isolated and connected scenarios. This approach, which incorporates local and non-local degrees of freedom, is capable of capturing thermal correlations that decay at a rate of $e^{-T}$ and is shown to be optimal in the high-temperature regime. When combined with the bond renormalization technique, this new method achieves $1/T$ precision and is capable of efficiently representing thermal states, as demonstrated through its application to a bosonic Hubbard model.

We have developed a decoupling theory for restricted performance measures, particularly applicable to cases where information is only available after a certain threshold has been met. This concept of decision-making based on limited effectiveness can be linked to the theory of decoupling. We have demonstrated that restricted performance measures can be effectively approximated by a collection of decoupled evaluations, and that these approximations are optimal in a sense that they minimize a specific risk function. Furthermore, we have derived an explicit formula for the optimal decision-making strategy and demonstrated its connection to a collection of risk functions. This framework provides a foundation for effective risk management in complex systems.

We introduce anisotropic $p$-capacitance for compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ along with a corresponding anisotropic Cheeger-Fuglede-McShane inequality that incorporates boundary flux. This new definition of anisotropic $p$-capacitance builds upon existing frameworks, including those by anelastic and elastic Hele-Shaw type capacities. We demonstrate the convergence of this capacity to limiting measures and establish an anisotropic Riesz representation theorem. Moreover, we prove a anisotropic Minkowski inequality of type Orlicz-spherically convex Saksman-Vuorinen from an variational perspective, demonstrating its connection to anisotropic $p$-capacity through an anisotropic trace inequality.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring the acceleration of two test masses made of different materials as they orbit the Earth. According to the principle, both masses should experience the same acceleration, but a difference in acceleration, known as a signal at the relative acceleration, would disprove the principle. However, the test masses can also experience non-equivalent forces unrelated to the principle, which can obscure any potential violation. To accurately determine the test's sensitivity, we need to account for the effect of instrumental noise and glitches. In this study, we used data from the Microscope mission to estimate the test's sensitivity and found that the level of noise and glitches limits the test's sensitivity to a specific level of violation.

Self-assembling structures in fluids gain significant interest due to their potential for fabricating complex materials at the micro and nano scales. A common approach to create "colloidal molecules" involves attaching a secondary particle to a primary one using a short-range connection, a design that works well under static conditions. However, when dynamic interactions are involved, the situation becomes more complicated. Our research focuses on understanding how these pairs behave when placed in an environment with varying levels of activity. We observe that active bonds linking the particles can lead to a variety of distinct phases, including chains, clusters, and rings, with the ring phase being particularly stable and achievable through moderately dynamic bonds. The stability of the ring phase is influenced by the activity levels at which the particles are connected. Our findings offer valuable insights for the development of "colloidal molecules" that can self-assemble into complex structures.

Under the usual shortest path routing, the efficiency decreases as the network grows larger due to network congestion. To alleviate this, we introduce a new concept called strong shortest path collection under SPSR. This new concept seeks to find the smallest number of non-interfering routing solutions under SPSR k, where k is any positive integer. We have established that determining k-SPSR k for any graph is a challenging problem that falls into the category of NP-completeness. We have also identified k-strong shortest path collection sizes for various types of graphs, including cubic networks, cycles, and moebius ladders.

The color dipole gluon PDF, situated in the non-global logarithmic region, experiences infrared renormalon corrections that can't be negated, leading to an unavoidable large uncertainty in the small-x regime for this quantity. To address this short-distance issue, a new scheme is proposed to counter the influence of renormalons for the color dipole gluon PDF. A novel nonperturbative input is required for this proposed scheme, and a generic model is employed to estimate its effect on the color dipole gluon PDF using a perturbative conversion from the gluon PDF at the LHC's operating energy ranges. The resulting uncertainty is significantly reduced, by a factor of 10, in comparison to the original impact of the color dipole gluon PDF.

We investigate the frog model on rooted trees, specifically focusing on random and biased versions. Baudoin and Curien previously determined the critical density for the standard (unbiased) case as $d_\tau \approx 3.03610$ for all trees of any degree $\tau$. We prove that for both the biased and standard cases, the critical density $d_\tau$ is solely determined by the tree degree $\tau$, and for trees of any degree $\tau > 3$, $d_\tau$ is not constant.

We propose an innovative concept called the magnetophotonic surface lattice, which involves a photonic lattice integrated with bending waveguides and directed by a magnetic field. This novel structure exhibits unique properties where its photonic transmission behavior can be controlled, resulting in hysteresis and lattice-like photonic patterns. These patterns can be manipulated using the magnetic field, creating effects that don't affect reverse-field transmissions. This lattice could have significant applications in photonic devices, enabling direction-dependent optical transmissions. Our proposed design is robust against minor structural imperfections, making it a reliable and practical solution.

We have developed an innovative approach to utilize pre-existing knowledge from a decision-based black-box model and transfer its learning to a target task via a targetedTKA framework. Our approach can leverage knowledge from the black-box model about decision boundaries and explicit features, even when it comes from a different distribution, and without access to its internal workings. To accomplish this, we created a surrogate model and a novel loss function that guides the target model to replicate the behavior of the pre-trained model. Surprisingly, our results show that zero-shot transfer from decision-based black-box models is quite successful.

Researchers have measured the decay properties of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$, 
with a decay rate of $3.64\times 10^8$ and a significance of $6.2\sigma$. 
After analyzing the $\bar{D}^0$ decay mode $K^+ \pi^-$, 
the study also found evidence for the decay $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$, 
with an combined significance of $4.6\sigma$. 
Additionally, a ratio of the decay rates was measured for these two $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{(*)0} K^0_S$ decays, 
with a value of $0.84\pm 0.07\pm 0.04$.

Building the lattice of submodules of a lattice-ordered module is a challenging task, and for group modules, there's a particularly difficult obstacle. We've developed an algorithm that takes the meet and join operations, along with the lattice meet of submodules, and successfully constructs the lattice of submodules of a group module that has a simple structure where no composition factors are repeated. However, it's important to note that this algorithm's efficiency heavily relies on the size of the module and may become impractical for modules of higher multiplicities.

A set of vertices $R$ in a graph $G$ is considered a robust geodetic set if it uniquely identifies all other vertices in $G$ based on the shortest paths between them, given that $R$ already knows a subset of edges on those shortest paths. Identifying the minimum robust geodetic set is called the minimum robust geodetic recognition problem. This study investigates the computational complexity of solving this problem for various classes of graphs, showing that it is solvable in polynomial time for outerplanar graphs and certain split graphs, but is NP-complete for chordal graphs, AT-free graphs, and some triconnected cubic graphs. Additionally, an upper bound for the problem in maximal planar graphs is shown to be fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the target solution size.

When it comes to complex tasks, obtaining expert demonstrations for learning is often impractical, resulting in expert behavior being suboptimal. This issue becomes even more significant in high-dimensional settings. To tackle this problem, we introduce a new framework that combines imitation learning with stochastic optimization under assumptions of realizability and bounded stochastic noise. Our key innovation is a modified version of Fitted Value Iteration, called TRAIL, which effectively manages noisy data. Under certain conditions, TRAIL converges to an $\epsilon$-optimal policy at a rate of $\frac{\sqrt{|\mathcal{S}|}}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{D}|}}$, where $|\mathcal{S}|$ is the state space size and $|\mathcal{D}|$ is the number of available experience tuples. Notably, our research reveals a fundamental limitation in traditional algorithms like Fitted Value Iteration under this new setting. In contrast, TRAIL's performance can be up to $\sqrt{|\mathcal{S}|}$ times better, and we provide theoretical insights into why value-based methods struggle in this scenario.

Reinforcement learning can be efficiently improved through imitation training, which utilizes a beneficial lesson learned from an expert. Nonetheless, obtaining and utilizing this lesson demands the collection of large-scale data by skilled professionals, which is both costly and impractical for many applications. In this research, we introduce a novel imitative framework that effectively utilizes small amounts of available information and prevents the algorithm from following undesirable expert behavior. We developed a flexible demonstration strategy that can be easily adapted to different scenarios and can even take the form of a simple, pre-existing model. Our method is further enhanced with a new training approach that enables successful outcomes even when the expert's data is insufficient. We validated our method's effectiveness through extensive testing on multiple public datasets and a large-scale reinforcement learning task.

This research focuses on the calculation of the distance and number of possible combinations for the p-adic convex hull, specifically the minimum distance between any two points. We begin by establishing a connection between the p-adic convex hull's structure and the maximum distance between any two points. Next, a general formula for determining the number of points is derived, along with an exploration of its implications. A set of recurrence relations is introduced to facilitate the calculation of the p-adic convex hull's structure and point distribution. Finally, the calculation of the volume is addressed, with an example using a balanced p-ary simplex highlighting the challenges involved.

Using a pre-trained translation model and fine-tuning it with reinforcement learning has been shown to enhance output quality.  However, the computational cost of evaluating each action during fine-tuning limits the number of available actions and thus the effectiveness of the process.  We've examined the expense of assessing translations as potential actions and have proposed a method to reduce this expense by limiting the action space to a few candidate actions.  We've also investigated the use of distillation to accelerate the evaluation process.  In our experiments, we've demonstrated that this approach can be applied to sentences with a large number of words.  Furthermore, we've found that our method allows for a more thorough application of different reinforcement learning algorithms.

A cost-effective and versatile solution for industrial robots is a Depth Camera, which offers precise 3D position data of objects gripped by the robot's end-effector. However, due to various factors, an uncalibrated camera can result in inaccurate pose and object position estimation. This paper presents an innovative method to calibrate the camera and estimate the pose by utilizing a single marker and machine learning techniques. Our approach involves initially collecting a dataset of images with a specific marker and employing a neural network to determine the end-effector's pose and the camera's calibration parameters. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we provided theoretical analysis and conducted numerical simulations, as well as performed real-world experiments with an ABB IRB 14000+ industrial robot and a Kinect v2 Depth Camera.

This study introduces the concept of QFS-region and its related matrix, along with novel attributes of QFS-rank and QFS-region. Several key properties of QFS-region are demonstrated, namely the inequality q(A) + (n - r(A)) ≥ n, the equivalence between conditions (1) and (2), and the derivation of the QFS-rank for specific matrix types, including nonnegative definite, positive semidefinite, and idempotent matrices.

The rise of online news consumption is accompanied by growing evidence of increasing polarization. Studies suggest that the online environment exacerbates pre-existing political divisions, which in turn negatively affects the overall consumption of online news. Our research leverages extensive datasets from major online news providers in the U.S., the U.K., and Australia to examine how political division in online news readers varies across different populations. We uncover several significant findings, including the observation that online news consumers tend to be politically inclined, with a significant portion exhibiting high levels of political division. We also detect distinct consumption patterns associated with different political stances, which we interpret through the lens of Self-Categorization Theory. Notably, we observe that partisan online news consumers exhibit stronger in-group preferences compared to their non-partisan counterparts. Our results further demonstrate that political division in online news consumers is consistently lower across different countries and news sources, with a significant portion of highly divided consumers belonging to specific demographic groups. Our research has important implications for the news industry and potential avenues for future investigation.

We investigate the word problem of the Thompson group V, which can be decomposed into V = V(Γ), where V is a one-parameter family of finitely presented groups that are epimorphically ordered, with some members isomorphic to the classical R. Thompson group V and others containing F as subgroups. We provide a scattering reduction system for V(Γ), and use it to prove that the word problem of V(Γ) has a uniformity index of 2 for all Γ. We also examine subgroups of V(Γ) defined by finite graphs, showing that their word problems have varying uniformity indices, which implies that the word problem of V(Γ) has a uniformity index of at least 2.

The nonequilibrium steady state of a driven quantum system can be studied through a quantum master equation.  A key aspect of this analysis is the steady-state density matrix, which is typically obtained by solving the quantum master equation.  We present both experimental and theoretical results for a driven superconducting qubit, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.  In the experiment, a precisely controlled microwave pulse drives a superconducting transmon qubit, and measurements of its response are made.  We compare our results to a theoretical model of a driven two-level system, which is derived from the full quantum dynamics.  This model accounts for the effects of the environment and the periodic drive, and allows us to accurately predict the nonequilibrium steady state of the qubit.  Our findings demonstrate the ability to experimentally access the density matrix of a driven quantum system and accurately characterize its steady-state behavior.  This has important implications for the development of new quantum technologies, which rely on the precise control of quantum states.

We explore how certain complex structures, 2-forms, and scalar functions that follow specific periodic patterns influence the biharmonic behavior of hypersurfaces in Euclidean space. This investigation focuses on submanifolds where these elements obey a power of Laplacian-related transformations and fixed or varying assignments, ultimately demonstrating how such conditions necessitate the biharmonic nature of the defined hypersurfaces within their ambient space.

Given a positive integer q greater than 1, and a fraction p between 0 and 1 exclusive, if the base-q representations of nonnegative integers, when truncated to n digits, can be used to accurately determine a specific set A from all n-tuples in base q after sufficiently many Truncations, then A is referred to as (p,n,q)-identifiable. If this process works for any sufficiently large n, then A is referred to as (p,q)-identifiable. We provide a general framework for (p,q)-identifiable sets, along with several straightforward applications, and specifically, if p and q are relatively prime, we can rephrase (p,q)-identifiability in terms of the base-q representation of any element. Moreover, we can identify the smallest and largest (p,q)-identifiable sets, and the sets consisting of all numbers whose base-q representations only contain the digits p and p+1 immediately preceding them.

The observed discrepancy in the Sun's rotation curve can be attributed to a yet-undiscovered form of matter residing in the Galactic Center, the result of a phenomenon where the gravitationally bound axion stars in the center of the galaxy gradually transformed into dense stars composed of sterile neutrinos due to the emission of sterile neutrinos. This process, which occurs at a rate of $10^{42}$ GeV$^{-1}$ per second, leads to an object with the characteristics of a dark star made of sterile neutrinos with a radius of approximately 30 kilometers. The presence of such an axion-neutrino hybrid star could potentially be detected through the observation of a distinctive phase in the light curve of its parent axion star. Furthermore, the unique gravitational waves emitted by these objects during collisions or mergers may provide an additional means of detection.

The LAMOST Time-Domain Survey (LTDS) will utilize 4 $K$2 plates to conduct a comprehensive analysis, including an examination of the $ATc$2 sample, which consists of approximately 55 million stars, over the course of one year. The project's design is based on the LAMOST $ATc$2 and the LAMOST 2-degree Wide-Survey (LWS2), and will take advantage of the $K$2 spectrograph's dual capabilities to perform high-precision astrometry and radial velocity measurements. The $K$2 spectrograph is capable of capturing 100 exposures per night, and the team plans to use 8 of these nightly observations to conduct the survey. The project will utilize a 12-month baseline survey to establish an initial framework, and will be able to identify about 500,000 exoplanets, 50,000 $asteroseismic$ variables, and 10,000 binaries. The data from the high-resolution spectra will also be able to provide information on stellar properties, chemical composition, and the ages of the sample. The project will be able to provide a comprehensive understanding of the $galactic$ structure, stellar populations, and the evolution of the $milky$ way. The LAMOST $ATc$2 sample will be divided into three regions, and the project will be able to provide a comprehensive analysis

This study introduces the edge-Gated CNN architecture, which is designed for high-precision, efficient, and fully connected semantic segmentation in medical imaging.
The innovative edge-Gated units integrate both long and short-range spatial dependencies, as well as semantic information from adjacent voxels, to enhance the accuracy of the segmentation process.
Experimental results on three benchmark datasets - Pannum, Sun Dataset, and KiTS19 - demonstrate the model's superiority over existing methods, achieving a mean Intersection over Union of 0.918, 0.891, and 0.838, respectively, with relatively low computational requirements.

We present a formal specification for MongoDB's transactional behavior,
which we validate using model checking to ensure correctness. As MongoDB lacks
available correctness proofs or transactional test cases, we employed TLA+ to
define and verify the consistency of its serial transactions. Focusing on
collection operations, we established that the order of executed transactions
preserves coherence. This allows us to identify bugs in the system's
implementation, which were successfully reported to the developers.

Hosono and Kim established a striking pattern in the chromatic symmetric functions involving powers of the variable $e$. We demonstrate that this pattern holds true for subsets of graphs within broader categories, such as outerplanar graphs and series-parallel graphs. Furthermore, we uncover a deeper connection between the observed pattern and the revised nonnegativity property in the inverse Kostka array from algebraic combinatorics.

To tackle complex tasks, humans and animals employ a range of cognitive functions,
among them is the executive function, which enables flexible adaptation to novel situations.
Building on a previously proposed biologically-inspired learning framework, we introduce a
hindsight summarization mechanism to guide value learning, and expand our model to include
this crucial aspect of cognition. Our approach integrates multiple perspectives on perception,
and we discuss the implications of our work within the broader context of the introduced model.

A major obstacle in training machine learning models for medical imaging is the potential presence of implicit bias in data sets. These hidden prejudices can lead to compromised performance and the unintentional reinforcement of stereotypes. To date, there has been limited research into identifying and mitigating implicit bias within medical image data sets. This study introduces a novel approach to innate bias detection, drawing on color bias as an illustrative example. We propose BiasNet, a network designed to identify implicit bias by training on a large data set of 1.2 million chest X-rays. Our proposed method leverages pre-trained neural network models to assess implicit bias in medical imaging data sets. This research is expected to pave the way for more reliable machine learning applications in medical imaging by addressing the issue of implicit bias.

This work delves into the hidden structural and dynamic aspects of intricate systems using a theoretical model, specifically examining spin reversal dynamics in complex assemblies where spins interact in both pairwise and triangular configurations. A bi-fractional random geometry is employed to represent this complexity, enabling analysis of spin reversal behavior through the lens of geometric entanglement. Notably, concealed properties of these complex networks significantly influence their dynamic patterns. Notable effects, such as non-monotonic variations in relaxation times, arise due to the underlying network structure and can be precisely predicted using a concealed degree distribution. Furthermore, comparison of reversal times across purely random and complex networks highlights a distinct effect attributed to the network's concealed geometry.

As the Sun's innermost companion, the PSP has begun its journey, with the probe's proximity to the Sun allowing for the measurement of the "Solar breeze" as it flows outward into the heliosphere. By combining the solar wind speed and density observed near the Sun by the PSP with solar irradiance measurements, the flux of energy carried by the Solar breeze can be determined. As the Solar breeze moves away from the Sun, its energy flux diminishes, following the characteristic pattern of radiative energy flux. However, observations reveal a notable deviation from this decrease when moving from the Earth's orbit inward, indicating the presence of additional structures within the Solar breeze that require further investigation.

Identifying speech emotions is a significant task in speech-emotion recognition, but obtaining labeled data is a common challenge. While label augmentation techniques exist, they often fail to accurately reflect genuine emotions. A common issue in EMO-21, a widely used speech-emotion recognition dataset, is the large discrepancy between training and testing data. To tackle this problem, we introduce a novel approach called Domain Adapting Deep Reinforcement Learning for speech-emotion recognition. This approach adapts the domain of data for testing without sacrificing the original information. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses the state-of-the-art performance on the EMO-21 dataset.

In this study, we used nuclear forward scattering to investigate the local structure and magnetic properties of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under high pressure up to 10 GPa. Our findings show that the compound undergoes a structural phase transition from P6$_3$ to P6$_3$/m at approximately 5.5 GPa. This transition is accompanied by the appearance of a structural doublet in the spectra, and the high-pressure spectra can be fully explained by the high-pressure structural data. Additionally, we observed that the magnetic doublets present in the low-pressure spectra gradually diminish with increasing pressure, and the magnetic splitting vanishes completely at around 4.5 GPa, correlating with the loss of long-range magnetic order.

This research addresses the sensitivity of discrete shortest path algorithms to rounding errors in edge lengths, resulting in bounded deviations from the true optimal route. These estimates are then utilized to refine the solution space in continuous shortest path problems, particularly in the context of limited-cruise-speed shortest time calculations. By formulating a simplified model of fixed-cruise-speed trajectory optimization between two fixed points, the study demonstrates how the algorithm's exactness properties can be applied to obtain an efficient, optimality-condition-based solver. The development of a customized Dijkstra-based algorithm for this model is presented, showcasing its ability to provide an optimal solution directly, rather than just a refined starting point for more complex optimization techniques.

Researchers have extensively studied the effects of intense shock waves on the universe,
particularly those moving at the speed of light, for their potential to communicate vast distances.
In this study, we investigate the behavior of a shock wave in a universe in expansion,
near a spherical void, and its impact on fluid communication.
In one-dimensional models, the reflection of shock waves allows for communication over longer distances,
but these models are unrealistic. Conversely, in three-dimensional models,
the intensity of the shock wave decreases after it passes a certain point,
thereby amplifying the wave's effect and enabling communication across even greater distances.

Using 3.0 inverse femtobarns of data from the CERN LHCb, the differential decay rate for $B_s^0 \rightarrow D_s^{*-} \mu^+ \nu_{\mu}$ was measured as a function of the $D_s^{-}$ momentum, after reconstructing the $D_s^{*-}$ from its decay products $K^- \pi^+$. The decay rate distribution was modeled using various parametric functions, with a two-component Chebychev polynomial providing the most statistically significant fit. The results are normalized to the total $B_s^0 \rightarrow D_s^{*-} \mu^+ \nu_{\mu}$ decay rate, and the absolute decay rate is also reported.

A new class of functions known as generalized Hermite polynomials is defined, which includes both classical Hermite polynomials and polynomially modified Hermite functions as special cases. These functions are shown to be connected to specific Schr\"odingal operators that admit unique, repeatable solutions. As a side note, the paper also provides an analysis of the long-standing conjecture regarding the relationship between classical Hermite polynomials and potential Schr\"odingal operators.

The sound produced when peeling adhesive tape through acoustic analysis yields insightful data. Peel spectra reveal the frequency distribution of noise intensity, while acoustic waveforms offer a glimpse into the micro-scale peeling process. A novel, high-speed optical system has been developed to investigate the mechanisms behind the acoustic signals, revealing that the noise arises from the asynchronous peeling of multiple fragments, with synchronization leading to sound synchronization and desynchronization leading to quiet periods. This finding bridges the gap between acoustic data and visual observations, offering valuable information about the peeling process' dynamics.

Our theoretical analysis posits that planar Josephson junctions and loops exhibit a distinct reentrant BCS state between two insulating phases, which we refer to as the CBCS state.  This predicted behavior is influenced by a long-range Coulomb interaction, which significantly alters the sequence of phase transitions from 1D systems to 2D systems based on gate voltage and temperature.  To test this prediction, we analyzed experimental data from multiple Josephson junctions and SQUIDs, which showed a corresponding reentrant pattern, and observed a similar sequence in the 2D system.  This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the critical boundaries in the phase diagram of 2D superconducting systems and highlights the unique properties of the CBCS state.

The addition of a specific term to the Standard Model, known as the "absolute scale ether-like term," can be understood through non-abelian gauge theories. By applying a non-perturbative approach called the closed-time-path effective action, the behavior of this term can be analyzed, particularly with respect to temperature. Calculations show that this term acquires a non-zero value due to thermal fluctuations and its inclusion leads to new daisy diagrams that correct the thermal masses of Standard Model particles. A key finding is that these corrections are governed by the strong interaction and may become dominant in certain scenarios. Additionally, the concept of Lorentz symmetry breaking associated with this term is challenged, as it may instead indicate the selection of a preferred frame of reference within the universe.

Under the assumption of continuously rebalancing delta hedging, the cost of trading options increases as the underlying asset is repeatedly purchased or sold. This research derives a formula for option margin that accounts for transaction costs resulting from delta hedging strategies, and is applicable to a broad range of strategies due to its development within the framework of Feller's generalized Brownian motion. The cost is determined by the price of a portfolio that results from selling the option and executing a delta hedging strategy that may include selling or buying the underlying asset, depending on the option's delta value. The formula is used to calculate option prices with cash accounts, and provides the necessary margin to prevent arbitrage opportunities. For instances where only buying the underlying asset is the optimal hedging strategy, the cost aligns with standard formulas, and the research presents the option price as a function of these costs. Additionally, the option's delta hedge ratio can be calculated by balancing the cost of maintaining a zero margin account and the benefits of reducing the required margin.

This research examines the effective properties of heterogeneous materials composed of two distinct phases, with differential constraints applied to one phase. We analyze the homogenization process for a specific class of periodic composite structures and derive an explicit formula for the resulting homogenized energy. Furthermore, our findings can be applied to understand the behavior of nanostructured metals and high-contrast metal-dielectric mixtures.

We've analyzed 103 early-type galaxies in the Subaru Prime-Survey that show signs of mergers, identified by irregular shapes or extended structures. By comparing this number to a large HSC sample of 150,000 early-type galaxies, we estimate that galaxies with visible tidal features make up about 10% of the population. These tidal structures are often too small to be detected by visual inspection. Using this 10% fraction, we calculate the major merger rate for early-type galaxies, which is 10% of all early-type galaxies per billion years. This rate is significantly lower than for spiral galaxies and the discrepancy becomes more pronounced at higher redshifts.

The success of a young professional is influenced by a variety of factors, including economic conditions and available opportunities in their field of work. This study seeks to examine how different scenarios can impact the career progression of young people and their offspring. A created model is employed to gather and analyze data, revealing that increased opportunities can positively influence career growth and reduce the impact of family background on an individual's success. Furthermore, it is found that fluctuations in the economy can result in increased inequality and reduced mobility, but targeted support can mitigate these effects.

The cutting-edge field of ultrafast laser technology has significantly
  revolutionized materials processing, making it possible to modify the
  physical and chemical properties of a wide range of substances.  Achieving high
  power ultrafast lasers necessitates a rigorous design of the laser system's
  components, particularly the gain medium, which is essential for effective
  materials control.  In this paper, we present an in-depth analysis of ultrafast
  laser systems, focusing on their interaction with various substances.  The
  discussion covers critical aspects such as ultrafast laser materials, their
  characterization, and the underlying principles of their design and reverse
  engineering.  The content is presented in a clear and accessible manner,
  suitable for both graduate students and professionals in the field.

We prove that for any incompressible subset K of $\ell_p$, where $1\le p<\infty$, and any arbitrarily small positive value $\varepsilon$, there exists a mapping from K into $\ell_{p_\delta}$ such that the distance between any two points in K is increased by no more than a factor of $p+\varepsilon$ while the image is contained within a ball of radius $d(K)+\delta$. Additionally, we show that for any incompressible subset K of $\ell_p$, the limit as $\varepsilon$ approaches zero from the right of $d_{\varepsilon}(K)$ is equal to $p$.

A new technique called the brightness scan has been introduced to beam diagnostics, which leverages the non-invasive method of recording a beam's profile as it moves across a target area. This technique leverages the available data from modern beam diagnostics systems that measure beam profiles, allowing for an efficient use of data without requiring additional scans. The technique is applicable to any beam diagnostics system that involves moving beams, including those using moving coils or flat targets. The brightness scan can provide valuable information about the beam's phase space properties, including its overall shape and any variations in density. A detailed explanation of the brightness scan technique is given, along with the conditions necessary for it to work effectively and necessary Data Analysis tools. The benefits of brightness scans are demonstrated through the analysis of data collected at the CERN Large Hadron Collider.

This paper introduces a distributed optimization method that enables each participant to find the optimal solution while keeping their information private. The method is robust against malicious attacks, where a malicious user tries to manipulate the system to achieve an optimal solution that benefits them. Theoretical analysis and numerical results demonstrate the convergence rate and accuracy of the proposed technique.

The precise measurement of the CMB power spectrum is significantly impacted by instrumental biases, whose accurate modeling is crucial for the successful interpretation of future high-precision observations. To address this challenge, a new framework has been developed, building upon the existing s4cmb code, enabling researchers to simulate future large-scale microwave background experiments such as the Simulated Stage-IV CMB Survey. This code is based on the existing s4cmb library and incorporates the ability to generate accurate, full-sky simulations of the microwave background, including cosmic reionization and primordial fluctuations, as well as the precise description of the instrument's response, including the scanning strategy and the instrument's ability to measure the microwave background. The code is designed to be modular and extensible, allowing for the inclusion of additional instrument models and simulation features, and is being made available to the scientific community through an open-source platform.

In NLP tasks, starting with a trained language model as a base has become the standard approach.  However, incorporating these models adds a significant computational cost.  As these models continue to grow in size, understanding their role can become challenging.  To address this issue, we focus on a single task to minimize extraneous variables.  Specifically, we examine the impact of using a trained language model in a simple word arrangement problem.  We find that for a basic version of this problem, a majority of participants can achieve a high level of success without a trained language model.  When the difficulty is increased, those who start with a trained language model as a base have a clear advantage.  Furthermore, we explore the role of pre-training on shorter texts.  We also investigate the effect of training the trained language model on the more difficult word arrangement problem.  We observe that models that were trained on simpler instances perform better on a more difficult version of the problem, when compared to models that were trained on a diverse range of texts.

Deepfakes are a type of deceptive media created using advanced production techniques and AI, which can mimic real people in video with startling ease. As deepfake technology continues to improve, it poses a significant threat to our online security, making the development of effective detection methods crucial. Our research proposes a novel deep learning framework called MD-CSDNetwork, which is capable of identifying deepfakes with high accuracy. This model combines several successful deep learning approaches and is particularly adept at handling subtle inconsistencies that are characteristic of GAN-based deepfakes. Experimental results demonstrate that our network achieves exceptional performance, including outstanding outcomes on multiple benchmarks, even with limited data.

Current research has extensively examined binary deletion channels in relation to random and structured bit-flip channels, yet studies specifically focusing on low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with binary deletion channels are still limited. We have analyzed the tripple-edge condition for a particular class of LDPC codes with degree-degree correlations, identifying it as sufficient to guarantee recoverability from binary deletions at a rate close to capacity. We have also demonstrated that this code class exhibits localized decoding behavior, allowing us to derive the code's tripple-edge condition in terms of its degree distribution and binary deletion profiles, and estimate its inner bound in terms of degree distributions.

When implementing a secure quantum key distribution network, the large number of central nodes necessitates an efficient method for directly generating secure keys between the sender and recipients. To mitigate existing vulnerabilities in this scenario, a new approach has been proposed that involves splitting the signal into multiple decoy states with varying phases randomly applied. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed method and calculates its secure key generation rate. The results show that the secure key generation rate significantly surpasses that of the original approach under specific loss conditions. The substantial increase in the key generation rate is achieved with minimal additional equipment requirements. The research results are applicable to both time-bin and polarization-based implementations of the proposed method.

Current mobile network management systems lack core network visibility, hindering effective performance and capacity optimization. This issue is exacerbated by the complex mix of network technologies and virtualization in future 5G networks. We investigate core network operation principles, performance factors, and design options, focusing on identifying and addressing problematic areas. We discuss potential solutions for enhancing core network monitoring and management, considering virtualization's role. Core network administration is crucial for overall network performance and should be included in self-organizing network concepts. We propose a set of core network management procedures and examine their feasibility and implementation challenges.

In the 1920s, Menger introduced the abstract angle concept and demonstrated its ability to incorporate fundamental Euclidean, Minkowskian, and spherical metric ideas. Although some researchers made contributions to the field, the overall development of angle theory has not been as rapid as other metric spaces subdivisions. This paper presents a diverse set of abstract angle operations and associated properties, utilizing the inspiration from subdifferential calculus, thereby expanding the initial ideas proposed by Menger.

We investigate the relationship between successive minima and lattice theory in number fields, deriving an upper bound on the ratio of the $(n+1)$-th and $n$-th successive minima that relates to the degree and discriminant of the number field. This upper bound has implications for understanding the structure of rings and orders in number fields. Specifically, we show that the maximal ideal size of a ring or order is exponentially bounded by its rank times the $(n-1)$-th successive minimum ratio. Moreover, this finding enables a new upper limit on the maximal ring size of a function field over a curve, which in turn leads to an upper bound on the $\mathfrak{a}$-Weil index of a curve.

We present a novel fs/ps hybrid 1D rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy method using two probes to achieve fast fs-scale pressure measurement and the overall O2/N2 ratio in a gas mixture. This technique enables the efficient use of a limited spectral range and overcomes the trade-off between the accuracy of temperature, pressure, and the O2/N2 ratio measurements. A dual-probe setup was created to minimize the bandwidth requirements and ensure the independence of the measurement channels. The probes' spectra were accurately measured using a fs pump and a ps probe with a tunable delay line, and a machine learning-based approach was applied to extract multiple variables simultaneously. The system was calibrated with precise temperature, pressure, and O2/N2 control, and the measurement accuracy was verified. Our approach achieves a 1.5% temperature measurement accuracy, 1.5x10^4 Pa pressure accuracy, and 0.1 O2/N2 ratio accuracy, and the probes' spectra can be easily integrated into a compact system for a wide range of applications.

The formation of planets within protoplanetary disks is hindered by the inefficient collection of gas and dust by small particles. One theory proposes that particles may form localized vortex structures in the outer regions of the disk, enhancing their ability to gather mass. A computational simulation was conducted to analyze a narrow annulus of the disk, exploring various conditions of particle interaction and gas flow. It was observed that under specific conditions, particles spontaneously form and maintain vortex structures, which can significantly slow down the rate at which particles drift towards the central star. Additionally, it was found that weak connections between particles can enhance the stability of these vortex structures. This discovery has important implications for the formation of planets within protoplanetary disks.

We investigate the linear response of a two-dimensional Fermi liquid to a small electrical voltage applied between two circular neutral points located at the corners of an annulus.  By calculating the equilibrium properties induced by this setup using a real-space approach, we find that neutral modes at the Fermi surface generate a low dc electrical conductance that is sensitive to the positions of the neutral points.  In a Landau–Lifshitz geometry, where the inner and outer circles are aligned, this conductance exhibits oscillations as the outer radius is varied.  These neutral-mode conductances can be understood through current-current correlations, which in turn are related to the fluctuations of the Hall drift experienced by an electron as it traverses a path between the inner and outer circles.

We leverage the Fock representation to establish that certain quantum group actions
on crystal varieties preserve open subsets isomorphic to other crystal varieties.
This enables us to extend the quantum group module structure from the global sections
to the sections of a line bundle on the quotient space $\mathcal{X}/U_q(\mathfrak{g})$.
Furthermore, we demonstrate the cluster character theory for the quantum $\mathfrak{sl}_n$
at $q=1$ and $q\neq 1$, respectively, by utilizing the quantum Grassmannian
$\mathcal{G}_{1,n}$ as the space of interest.

Deep learning models are frequently deployed to address issues across a wide range of applications, but they are typically trained using a central server that aggregates data and performs training. In contrast, we observe that many modern systems collect data and process it in a fully distributed manner, without the need for a central server. We propose a new decentralized training algorithm called DR-DSGD, which is suitable for these environments. This algorithm combines several key features, including a distributionally robust optimization framework and a decentralized update rule that takes into account the local data distribution. We provide theoretical support for DR-DSGD by proving convergence rates in terms of both accuracy and communication efficiency. Numerical experiments show that DR-DSGD converges faster than comparable decentralized methods and outperforms other graph-based approaches in terms of accuracy.

Researchers have long been interested in understanding how data is stored on hard drives using magnetic fields. To better understand this, various models have been developed to study the behavior of stored information. This review examines the key advancements in these models from the 1950s to the present day. It also highlights the significant role that hard-drive modeling plays in designing more efficient data storage systems.

This study investigates the initial state uncertainty impact on medium-modified jet data from the LHC, utilizing the pQCD framework for two-jet production and hadron production within a single jet at the LHCb and ALICE experiments. The findings indicate that the medium modification of hadron spectra within a jet remains largely unaffected by initial state uncertainty, with minor variations seen in two-jet data at LHCb. The analysis also reveals the need for nuclear PDF corrections in Pb-Pb data, with the EPS09 nuclear PDF set reducing the cross-section by approximately 10% and influencing scale dependence and medium modification ratios. Furthermore, increasing the initial state scale from 1 to 2 reduces the two-jet modification ratio by around 10% at LHCb, with similar effects observed in ALICE data. The increase in initial state scale has a minimal impact on hadron production within a jet and two-jet data at ALICE. The analysis shows that the medium modification ratio for two-jet data is about 10% higher in Pb-Pb data compared to pp data, with the scale effect reducing this difference to around 5%. The analysis finds that the medium modification ratio for hadron production within a jet remains largely unchanged in Pb-Pb data, with the medium modification ratio for two-jet data about 10-20% higher in Pb-Pb data than in pp data. A novel fraud technique, Forsage, was uncovered on the Ethereum blockchain in 2020. 
The scheme, which combines deceptive marketing with deceptive cryptocurrency technology, 
has been promoted through the use of social media platforms, such as YouTube and Facebook. 
The speed at which Forsage spreads is facilitated by the use of encrypted communication channels, 
such as Telegram, that obscure the involvement of users. 
The scheme's name originates from the incorporation of the word "crypto" into enticingly 
named products, such as Forsage's "Bio-Crypto." 
The method of payment for Forsage involves the use of gift cards, 
which are often purchased with borrowed money, thus concealing the true extent of the fraud. 
The creators of Forsage have been able to evade law enforcement by utilizing 
the decentralized nature of the Ethereum blockchain to process transactions. 
The scheme's success is due to the perceived legitimacy of smart contracts, 
which Forsage's creators claim are programmed to execute the terms of the agreement. 
The scheme's creators have been able to manipulate the code of the smart contract to 
their advantage, thus nullifying the blockchain's intended transparency. 
The rapid pace of Forsage's spread is due to the pyramid-like structure of the scheme, 
which rewards participants for recruiting new members. 
The scheme's success is also due to the use of data analytics to identify potential recruits, 
as well as the use of machine learning to predict user behavior.

We have conducted an examination of 19 previously identified and undocumented globular clusters in the bulge region of the Milky Way, utilizing the VISTA Variables in the Via Lactea (VVV) survey data. Our findings confirm the existence of nine of these objects, while the status of the remaining ten requires further investigation. Additionally, we discovered data inconsistencies in the 2009 VVv catalog and have provided a comprehensive list of cluster properties, encompassing variables such as total mass, half-light radius, and star formation history.

This study examines the dynamics of massive quark effects in Hadron-Hadron Drell-Yan processes. Unlike massless partons, massive partons do not have independent distribution functions, necessitating factorization into hadronic and universal parts. We extend the one-loop factorization formula for lepton-pair production to incorporate two-loop corrections for partonic cross-sections. We also examine the impact of higher-order corrections and initial-state parton coherence in processes resulting in lepton pairs and jet activity.

The accuracy of density functional theory is contingent on the choice of appropriate functionals, but this can be a time-consuming process. As an alternative, the reliability of tight-binding models for predicting optical properties has been investigated, despite their limited number of electrons being confined to atomic orbitals. A new tight-binding model has been developed and its validity assessed by comparing its optical properties to ab initio models and experimental data. The model's parameterization method is straightforward and based on the diagonalization of atomic Hamiltonians, along with a simplified description of electron-electron interactions. This approach is demonstrated using silicon as an example, and the resulting model matches optical data well, with only minor discrepancies. Notably, the model's invariance to the choice of measure has been confirmed, with only slight differences in performance observed between discrete and continuous measures.

We've developed a new class of quantum error correction codes that are invariant under a set of operations and can efficiently represent volume laws for entropy under certain conditions. This class of codes, which includes the harmonized entanglement renormalization ansatz (HE-RNA) and the hybrid invariant mirror entanglement renormalization ansatz (HIMERA), can also encode holographic information at a cost of logarithmic entropy loss. Building on the work of Pastawski et al., our codes are designed to be robust against erasures and can be used to achieve fast, holographic quantum error correction. Specifically, our invariant unitary HE-RNA and HIMERA states can be decoded using a classical algorithm with a time complexity of O(log^2 N), where N is the number of physical qubits. This code has the additional benefit of being able to correct a large number of qubits in a wide range of patterns, which is demonstrated through the use of a binary erasure channel and the mitigation of Heisenberg interactions.

A computational study was conducted to analyze the photoisomerization of retinal in bacteriorhodopsin using a quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical (QM/MM) approach. Retinal is responsible for vision in many animals and is found in rhodopsin. In this study, a modified potential energy landscape was developed to account for light energy and temperature effects on retinal. By statistically sampling this landscape, researchers were able to determine reaction rates for retinal in bacteriorhodopsin and observe how they change with temperature. They also found that bacteriorhodopsin stabilizes an unstable form of retinal and facilitates its conversion back to the original state. Furthermore, extreme temperatures were found to either inhibit or promote this reaction due to changes in the surrounding protein environment.

Deep-learning methods such as Long Short-Term Memory networks and Graph Convolutional Networks have shown great potential in process mining, a data-driven approach to understanding business processes. This paper critically examines the latest research using these technologies, highlighting the importance of carefully selecting models and metrics to avoid misleading conclusions. A case study is presented to showcase the advantages of deep-learning methods over traditional process mining techniques, with results indicating significant improvements in outcome prediction accuracy.

This research focuses on analyzing Twitter updates during the 2020 Izmir earthquake, which occurred on October 30, 2020. By applying text mining techniques to the 15000 posted messages, we identified the primary topics of interest to users following the earthquake. Furthermore, by examining the frequency of hashtags, we identified the key organizations that users were most concerned about.

We establish that several key properties of the Gaussian function are shared by elements of Gelfand-Shilov spaces. By leveraging this characteristic, we develop Fourier-based definitions and confirm the non-empty nature of these spaces. Furthermore, we apply these findings to investigate the continuity of specific operators, which can transform the Gaussian function into any given element of $C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$, resulting in characteristic functions within the spaces $S_\rho^\rho(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for $0<\rho<1$. This line of reasoning enables us to deduce the non-triviality of two types of subspaces, which consist of functions whose Fourier transforms also belong to $S_\rho^\rho(\mathbb{R}^d)$ or $S^\rho_\rho(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for the same value of $\rho$. In addition, we utilize these results to demonstrate that two particular classes of Toeplitz operators on the Segal-Berezin space do not equal the entire space.

Existing data from the event revealed significant changes in the star's brightness across different wavelengths, with a notable increase in the flux of the white-light flash and a subsequent decrease in the flux of the optical and near-infrared spectra. Our simulation of the effects of the flare on the star's continuum revealed that the effects of the flare would be most pronounced in the near-ultraviolet spectrum, with a notable increase in the flux of this spectrum following the white-light flash. Our data also suggest that the effects of the flare would be most severe on the star's surface in this spectrum, with a notable increase in the temperature of the star's surface in this spectrum.
